On Saturday, March 23, 2013 12:14:56 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
Given the location of the problem (DoubleVectorView), I don't think we should worry about this. Bob has been writing a replacement for it. 

I'm not good at reading these error messages. Is it possible the error is in the test and not the class? If so, could you take a stab at fixing it?

It doesn't look like a big problem. The class definition

  template<bool used, bool is_vec>
  class DoubleVectorView {
  public:
    DoubleVectorView(size_t /* n */) { }
    double& operator[](size_t /* i */) {
      throw std::runtime_error("used is false. this should never be called");
    }
  };


doesn't allocate any memory, so when the test triggers the std::runtime_error by using false, false as the template parameters and referencing [0], the memory checker barks. Is there any harm to making it like the true, false case?

  template<bool used, bool is_vec>
  class DoubleVectorView {
  private:
    double x_;
  public:
    DoubleVectorView(size_t /* n */) : x_(0.0) { }
    double& operator[](size_t /* i */) {
      throw std::runtime_error("used is false. this should never be called");
    }
  };

Then we run into another problem with MetaTraits.DoubleVectorView_true_true. If I leave uncommented this snippet

  var a_var(1);
  std::vector<var> a_std_vector(3);
  Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> a_vector(4);
  Matrix<var,1,Dynamic> a_row_vector(5);

  DoubleVectorView<true,true> dvv1(length(a_var));
  dvv1[0] = 0.0;
//  dvv1[1] = 1.0;
//  dvv1[2] = 2.0;
  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(0.0, dvv1[0]);
//  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0, dvv1[1]);
//  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0, dvv1[2]);


It barks when it tries to put 1.0 into dvv1[1] given that length(a_var) is 1. I'm not sure where you were headed here.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] g++ 4.8
parts:
All else being equal, fewer gripes are better.

I'm not too worried about warnings for classes
we know are right and can explain why we get false
positive warnings from the compiler. It'd be
better to fix them, but I don't want to do that at
the cost of using extra memory and an extra constructor
assignment call (the suggested fix below).

I might be able to fix this when I refactor by
specializing more aggressively. It can be tricky,
though, as the compiler requires the concept to be implemented,
but sometimes we won't use the implementation.

- Bob

On Saturday, March 23, 2013 1:14:10 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
All else being equal, fewer gripes are better.

I'm not too worried about warnings for classes
we know are right and can explain why we get false
positive warnings from the compiler.  It'd be
better to fix them, but I don't want to do that at
the cost of using extra memory and an extra constructor
assignment call (the suggested fix below).

I don't think it is a false positive. The test tries to access memory that isn't there, although it the first case it is intending to cause a runtime error. Maybe for that one, we can just turn off the memory checker

http://code.google.com/p/address-sanitizer/wiki/AddressSanitizer#Turning_off_instrumentation

But that is only documented for clang++.

Ben
